title: LLM Fingerprinting via Semantically Conditioned Watermarks
claim: Prior fingerprints rely on brittle, detectable query-key pairs; ours uses a semantic domain plus a statistical signal to be stealthy and robust.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: threat model, prior works, ours; ✗/✓ marks
description: The figure has three columns. The left column, "Threat Model", shows a model owner (OpenAI-style logo) training a model with fingerprints and sharing it. A hooded attacker steals it and deploys it behind a malicious API. A dashed box lists the modifications the attacker can apply: unedited, sampling, quantization, pruning, finetuning and active defenses, each shown as a small robot icon. The middle column, "Prior works", shows an API query with a gibberish prompt that gets a odd fingerprint response and a green check. A filtered reply, "I can't help you", gets a red X. Below it are the boxes "Query-Key brittle" and "❌ Stealthy / ❌ Robust". The right column, "Ours", shows a French prompt and a French story response with a check. Below are "Semantic Domain" + "Statistical Signal" boxes, then "✅ Stealthy / ✅ Robust". Red and green marks carry the contrast.
caption: Illustration of Model Fingerprinting Left: The model owner trains and releases a model in which they have previously embedded a fingerprint. A malicious deployer modifies the model and deploys it behind an API without honoring its restrictive license. Right: In prior work, fingerprint detection relies on specific query-key pairs, which are neither stealthy nor robust to most deployment scenarios. We propose to use semantic domains (e.g., French) and statistical signals (e.g., semantically conditioned LLM watermarks), making the fingerprint stealthy and consistently detectable.
abstract: Most LLM fingerprinting methods teach the model to respond to a few fixed queries with predefined atypical responses (keys). This memorization often does not survive common deployment steps such as finetuning or quantization, and such keys can be easily detected and filtered from LLM responses, ultimately breaking the fingerprint. To overcome these limitations we introduce LLM fingerprinting via semantically conditioned watermarks, replacing fixed query sets with a broad semantic domain, and replacing brittle atypical keys with a statistical watermarking signal diffused throughout each response. After teaching the model to watermark its responses only to prompts from a predetermined domain e.g., French language, the model owner can use queries from that domain to reliably detect the fingerprint and verify ownership. As we confirm in our thorough experimental evaluation, our fingerprint is both stealthy and robust to all common deployment scenarios.
